Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, second left, LoP in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, second right, party leader Sonia Gandhi and others during the official launch event for her memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, in New Delhi,on Monday, November 16 | Photo Credit: Special arrangement
Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP) chairperson Sonia Gandhi on Monday (November 16, 2026) said the title of her memoir captured her journey towards finding a sense of belonging and acceptance in India, and her son, Rahul Gandhi , recalled that after the assassination of his father and former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, the people of the country had embraced his mother, telling her: “You belong to us.”
They were speaking at the official launch of her book, Belonging: A Journey of Love , in New Delhi in the presence of top Opposition leaders, including Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay , Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav , Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren , and Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah . However, no representatives from the Left parties attended the event.
BJP leader and former Punjab Chief Minister Capt. (retd) Amarinder Singh, known to be close to the Gandhi family, was seated in the front row. Also in attendance were former Vice President Hamid Ansari; Gursharan Kaur, the widow of former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh; former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar; former Finance Minister P. Chidambaram; and former National Security Adviser Shivshankar Menon, among others.
Ms. Gandhi said she wrote the memoir partly because there had been a lot written about her family that was untrue, and she wanted to set the record straight. “So much has been said about my family — mother-in-law, husband, son, daughter — most of it is unreal stories woven around you. Hurtful things are said. This is a way of bringing out my feelings and about my family,” she said.
Though the event was meant to avoid political references, there was unmistakable political messaging of Opposition unity at the event.
Speaking about the recent student-led Gen Z protests, Ms. Gandhi said it was most encouraging that young people were coming together to demand their rights. “Rather than advising them, we should take their advice,” she said.
Explaining the title of her book, Ms. Gandhi said it reflected how hard she had tried to belong after coming to India and marrying into the Gandhi family.
“It is also the case with so many women in India; when they marry, they may be from the same background, but it is difficult for women to adjust to their new household,” she said in a question-and-answer session with publisher HarperCollins’ Poulomi Chatterjee.
She recalled that her upbringing in Italy had taught her to respect elders, helping her adjust to the formal surroundings of the Gandhi household. Initially terrified of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, she took time before she could address her as “mummy”.
She said Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and her friend Manjulika Dubey, had persuaded her to write the book, though she had been reluctant to share her innermost feelings. “At the beginning, it was difficult, but once I started, the dam burst,” she said. The most difficult portions dealt with the assassinations of Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi, she noted.
VIDEO | Delhi: Explaining why she decided to write her memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love', Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi says much has been written about her family, including her mother-in-law, husband, son, daughter and herself, but most of it is far removed from reality. "Stories are woven around you. Untruths are woven around you, hurtful things are said which are nowhere near the truth. And I thought, well, perhaps this is a way of bringing out my feelings, what I know of my family, and maybe people will be sort of open to listen to my story too," she said.
Recalling her relationship with Rajiv Gandhi, she described their romance as magical. She had initially opposed his entry into politics, fearing it would take away their time together.
After his death, she said, she became like a child, while her children took on the role of parents.
In his speech, Mr. Rahul Gandhi spoke of his parents’ bond and recalled how he and his then-girlfriend visited the Varsity restaurant in Cambridge, where his parents had met, years later.
Narrating an episode from his own visit with his girlfriend, he said the staff there remembered his parents. When he asked the waiter what he should order, he was recommended chicken chasseur. “If you want to fall in love, go to Varsity restaurant. But never eat the chicken chasseur — the food is horror,” he said, drawing laughter.
Mr. Gandhi said he had grown up watching his parents share an unusually close relationship, with his mother often sitting on his father’s lap during meals. That world was shattered by the assassinations of his grandmother and father.
He said though his mother changed with the “flame of her life” going out, another door had opened through the people of India.
“I am not talking about the 50-70 haters. I am talking about the millions of people in the villages that my mama mentioned. They suddenly turned around and told her that you belong to us,” he said.
Mr. Gandhi said his mother had survived cancer four times, adding that she had never shown fear or backed down. “Not once in my life have I seen her scared,” he said.
“Mummy, Papa loved you, but I cannot even tell you how proud he would be of you,” he added.
